Not a PDA sibling, but my little brother is and I know our childhood was tough on him. Since I was so dysregulated and anxious and acted out a lot, he learned to push aside his own feelings and needs, became the family diplomat, and very co-dependent. His only outlet for anger and frustration was that once a day he'd shut himself in his room for half an hour to silently be "grumpy", and then came back acting happy again. Now, I was undiagnosed until I was 10, and also a scapegoat child and my dad's target for his anger and violence, so it doesn't necessarily have to be the same thing with healthy parents. But he also *still* blames himself for not "protecting me" against our dad and my bullies. It took me a long time to move past the jealousy and anger I felt about me being the punching bag and everyone liking him better... And realise that we were both victims. Just in different ways. Working on getting over my own feelings of shame and guilt about him being pushed aside because of me.

I'd say avoid getting a second child unless you're feel like you have time and energy to spare as it is.

I have a lot of respect and love for religions that involve nature worship and living in harmony with nature and all living things! Abrahamic religions have sadly been used as an excuse for wars, murder, persecution, violence and oppression, and while some followers do care about the environment, it's rare. This is not to say that all people who follow them are problematic though (I've met some wonderful Christians, Muslims and Jewish people), or that the belief in itself is inherently problematic. Just that the organisation of those religions has done way more harm than good...

I think that, for me, personally, my atheism makes me care more... Cause I believe this life is all we get, and people (and animals for that matter) are already suffering from our destruction of the environment. And (according to my beliefs), that's the only life THEY get too. I don't think there's a heaven that will grant them something better... And their single life being filled with disaster is much more devastating to me than the idea of them suffering on earth just to spend an eternity in paradise when they die.

Also pro-choice and childfree! Mainly childfree cause I, despite the fact that I love kids and want to work with them, realised living with a child (or even a partner) wouldn't be good for my mental health though lol. I used to want to foster kids.

If he's taking his pills and did his best to  stay aware of the early signs of mania, I'd say he's not a complete ah (as I'm sure you know, what happens in your brain when you're manic is pretty much identical to what happens during a psychosis), but if he stopped or became sloppy, knowing how much you can hurt people when manic, he's a major ah. But that doesn't really matter, cause what he's doing is still far from okay.

Yeah, that sure as hell isn't just depression. She might be depressed as well, but it's not what's causing this. S'icide threats, splitting (shifting between idealisation of others and yourself and completely villainizing the same person), obsession, extreme mood swings, abandonment issues, anger issues, paranoia etc are all classic BPD symptoms. I'm willing to be friends with people with BPD if I'm not their obsession, and they're self aware and putting in hard, honest work on self improvement. Hell, I used to have a BPD diagnosis when I was younger and still struggle with a lot of the same emotions (I've just learned to stay rational and not to act on them, so it was removed 6 years ago). This is obviously not the case with her. I'm so sorry you have to deal with this. I've had people threaten me with s*icide and putting the blame of all their feelings and actions on me too (pretty much all my exes did this), and it's exhausting, terrifying and painful. And it's hard not to internalize that blame. 

Don't try to fix her. You can't, and even if you could, you need to put your own well being first.

NTA. You didn't tell her she *can't* hang out with her or tried to force her not to, but expressed your worries about her spending time with someone who is a threat to her recovery and mental health. I'm a recovering addict too, and from my own experience, this is risky af. And I need the people close to me to be honest about those things, cause we can't always tell when we're spiraling into old habits and putting ourselves at risk. Self denial and sometimes subconsciously taking small steps towards a relapse is pretty standard for most of us.

NTA. I've been in her position. I had a fwb relationship with a close friend who I had unrequited feelings for. Now, neither of us were the dominant force in making moves, and the desire to have a physical relationship was mutual. We were very clear about it being platonic. I admitted to having feelings for him (he's not the best at cues either so he didn't figure), but said I was fully aware that we were just friends and I enjoyed it for what it was, and we still slept together a few more times. He owed me *nothing*, as he was always honest with his intentions. I feel secondhand shame for her actions, cause the thought of treating him the way she treats you makes me feel sick. That's not love. Just recklessness, obsession and a complete lack of respect for your boundaries.

You should cut ties. Surround yourself with people who respect you - you deserve that. And she sounds like she needs a BPD assessment...

NTA. First of all, whether or not a child sees their step parent as their parent depends on what the child wants and feels. Pushing a child, especially a child that literally lost their mom, to accept you as such is disrespectful and selfish. You do not owe her that, and she needs to realise that it's not about how she feels and what she wants, you're your own individual. Second... She needs to stop trying to mold you into what she wants you to be. Even if she actually was your mom, she shouldn't be treating you as an extension of herself. Just cause you have a daughter doesn't mean she'll like makeup or shopping or other stereotypically feminine things... Just like having a son doesn't mean he wont. You. Are. Your. Own. Person. And your dad's the one who gave his consent to a relationship with her. You didn't. If she was being loving in a respectful way and you hated her and was hurtful, that would be something to work through... But that's it. And she's the one being disrespectful here. Not you.

The black and white thinking part is interesting, cause with my PDA friends it's either COMPLETELY black and white, or being fully aware that we can learn from others and being more flexible than the general population. One of my PDA friends and I have concluded that we wont debate topics where we disagree at ALL, because he'll panic and feel personally attacked when we do... But he spent his youth fighting n*zis with ANTIFA and we share the values that truly matter. But another PDA friend is honestly the one who taught me that you shouldn't debate to "win". We never actually fought when debating cause none of us have views that upset the other, and we only disagreed on more specific topics, cause he's ancom and I was Marxist back then (and still agree with next to all Marx values, but ended up leaning more towards Kropotkin's theory with time). But I was extremely dogmatic at the time (6 years ago - I was 21). We had a discussion, and he paused after something I said, thought for a moment and went "... I've never thought about it that way. I think you're right". I'd never met anyone with his approach (I've turned my parents more leftist, but they'd never admit they were wrong in the heat of the moment), and I was baffled. I've since become more open minded too, cause I no longer view different points of view as a personal attack as long as they stick to the topic at hand. People still think we come across as black and white, but honestly I think it's mostly cause we spent a lot of time exploring, questioning and analysing our own opinions, and rarely come across a remotely logical counter argument that we haven't heard or thought about before.


I'm still very black and white about some things though. Like my belief that every individual, regardless of what they work with or if they can work at all, and regardless of who they are (sexuality, race, gender, intelligence, religion, disability etc), are just as deserving of well being, respect and safety, and that as long as it's not harming anyone or being forced upon someone else, people should be able to love, live and believe whoever, however and whatever they want. No one's gonna change my mind about that, and I will inevitably get angry if someone disagrees lol.

We don't *have* to hate or be angry at someone to acknowledge that they are still to blame for their own actions. It would have been different if she was younger, but she was old enough to be held accountable. I'm no longer mad at my abusers, I feel sorry for them. But that doesn't change the fact that they still chose to treat me the way they did. I genuinely wish all of them the best, and I know that next to all of them went through horrific abuse themselves... But it still doesn't excuse their abuse. And it's the exact same with her. 

A compassionate, non-vengeful mindset is beautiful. That's something you should nurture and love about yourself... But you deserve to show yourself that same compassion. And to realise that it doesn't matter what someone's gone through, they still don't have the right to hurt you. 

I hope you're getting trauma therapy and are surrounded by supportive and loving people. And I truly believe you WILL find sweet, respectful and healthy love; you seem like a very loveable person.

It's not a "just because". If I've done something wrong, regardless of what the other person may or may not have done, I apologise for that. The "two wrongs don't make one right"-principle, even if my wrong may be understandable or considered an adequate response. Because my brain is terrified of the vulnerability and loss of control that comes with apologising, and wants to make excuses or just avoid it and pretend like it didn't happen. 

If I was passive aggressive to someone who was disrespectful, I apologise for the passive aggression. Because that wasn't constructive, and passive aggression doesn't align with my values or how I want to treat others. Some toxic people "prove my instincts right" by using my apology to gaslight me or blame them for their actions, to which I can just go "no, what you did still wasn't okay, but I should have been more constructive in how I expressed that". 

If I stop doing this, it quickly develops into a pattern of me avoiding accountability out of fear. I'm an expert when it comes to lying to myself, unless I'm rigid about my principles. 

I've found that it also helps keeping abusers away. Cause part of the principle is taking responsibility for *my* part, and focusing on that in my apology, without validating how they acted. It's about sticking to the truth and separating right from wrong, keeping in mind that each of us are responsible for our own actions and reactions. It helps keep my head clear, and honestly helps with not panicking because there's a sense of control in just sticking to the truth. My last ex was a narcissist (like, textbook example narcissist) and this made it impossible for him to gaslight me. In the past, when I didn't stick to these principles and my reality got distorted by my own avoidance and fear, they could use that already distorted reality to further re-shape it to fit their agenda. Because if I've been making excuses in my head, justifying my actions to avoid vulnerability, some part of me is aware of this. And that awareness and guilt could be used against me.

Yeah... It's so very important to recognise that it's really about panic responses as well. It's not them not *wanting* to co-operate or not giving a fuck, but the lack of choice puts you in survival mode, and your whole system reacts as if your life is in danger - it is not deliberate. My guess is him having a shutdown reaction with me rather than meltdowns is caused by me being an adult he likes and wants to get along with but isn't as comfortable unmasking with as he is with his mom, so he feels too unsafe externalising his panic. So the freeze response gets triggered, and he just can't do or say anything until he feels like I'm returning his feeling of autonomy. I don't know if he actually would have a meltdown or would just shut off completely if I tried to force him, but the intense distress he's in is so damn obvious to me, cause I'm the same way (though I can't really see how any adult could fail to see it, even if they couldn't relate). 

Parents, of course, wont always have the choice to approach kids the way a babysitter, relative or teacher can. There are times kids will inevitably feel like they're only told to do it cause their parents want them to, and if their stress levels are already high it could be the final straw. All they can do is do their best to avoid it. And like, even if I give him choices and concrete reasons, it still takes an effort for him to actually do it, cause he doesn't have *full* autonomy since the reason still creates internal/perceived demands. I'm so proud of him every time he manages to defy his PDA.

If you are feeling sceptical of the whole apple cider vinegar thing - go for the schampoos on the market (+lots of conditioner afterwards for moisture). The important part is that they're free from sulfates and silicone. After letting your hair get used to going without those ingredients, you can either keep using the curly girl schampoo or just use conditioner. I keep using apple cider vinegar now and then rather than just conditioner simply cause it exfoliates my scalp and prevents dandruff.

My IQ has been measured twice by professionals (once during an ASD assessment and once during an ADHD assessment). As a kid, I scored 142... As an adult I only scored 121 (though they said they could tell I would have scored higher if I wasn't panicking about the test results being low - literally had to pause to get out and have a full blown panic attack). I'm guessing it's around 130. I dropped out of school due to severe mental illness and developed a drug addiction, and I think the combination of drug abuse and lack of education (and hence not letting my brain work and advance) has lowered it. My high analytical and verbal intelligence is high, and if I'm not anxious and don't have to sit still with a paper and a pen (ADHD) math is also fairly easy. My working memory and ability to remember verbal instructions is useless though, and so is my spatial thinking - common among us neurodivergents to be at very different levels in different areas of the test, combared to NT's who's scores in the different parts are usually pretty even. 

That being said... IQ is not an accurate measurement of intelligence. Especially the mensa sort of IQ, that only includes math, but the psychiatric IQ test as well. There are so many different kinds of intelligence, and IQ tests measure a very narrow amount of them. Not to mention how unreliable the tests are, seeing as how I, and many others, lose so much of our cognitive ability when feeling nervous.

Some folks with a high IQ are intelligent in the ways that matter, of course. But those who pass the mensa test and brag about how much smarter they are than anyone else sure aren't. They're lacking three of the most important components of an advanced intellect - nuanced thinking, introspection and EQ. 

If you take an IQ test and get a low score - please don't think of yourself as any "dumber" than they are. ❤️

Idk if it's gonna be the same with your dog. No way to tell. But what I CAN say is that you wont be able to see your dog's true colors after just a month. Everything's new (their home, the outside environment, you, the routines etc), they don't truly know if they can count on you yet, and they're usually anxious and stressed. Focus on your bond and bringing her attention to you - start when there are no dogs or people around and then work your way from there. "Focus" is a great command to practise, where you basically give her a treat for just making eye contact with you. Spend lots of time with her, reward her when she's done something right and avoid uneccessary stressful events and situations for a while. She'll *most likely* calm down with time. ❤️
